segments.description: Have you ever experienced burnout? Has anyone that's in full-time tennis not that you know of? It's a big question. It's a big question. It's a question that I hear all the time. Now, my name is Dan Keenan and I'm absolutely delighted to be with you here at the Tennis Australia, Australian Open Conference. And I'm not standing in front of you here today as an expert in the area of burnout. I don't proclaim to be a psychologist. Or am I here to tell you how you should think? But I will be sharing what I hope is a thought-revoking short presentation on an area that's becoming more and more important in our sport in the year of 2026. And we're going to look at burnout. Is it really an issue? Is it something that we can count as? Is it something we can come together as an industry to try and get a hold of? And are you thinking in these ways? Now, a little note that I would like to make is today's presentation, you're going to see a lot of pictures. It's not going to be a lot of words that are on the screen, but every picture has a meaning. Everything that I've hopefully brought together today is something that means something to me that I hope that can be thought-provoking for you. Now, the reality is, and I'm an international tennis academy owner, sort of tennis academy in Spain. I'm also someone that has the opportunity to be working at the highest level of the game. I'm currently bringing this to you from Riyadh, you know, where I'm at the WTA finals, working with some of the best doubles players in the world.

And I hear more and more, I'm burnt out. You know, you ask the question, how are you doing? How's things? Everyone doing okay? And the answer is, yeah, I'm okay, but I'm a little bit burnt out. Now, that is more and more what we're hearing. Now, is that the real deal? Is that truly what's happening? We don't know. The reality is, we are seeing growing numbers, you know, burnout is developing, you know, recently Forbes. Now, this is not just tennis specific, but people have a job burnout at 66% in 2025 in this new study. Now, I would argue in tennis, it's even higher, you know, with the long days, the long hours, the weekend work, the high expectations. You know, bills are going up for everybody. Social media is in our face. There's a comparison. You know, the comparison is the thief of joy, you know, as we're comparing ourselves to what everyone else is doing around the world. You know, it builds up peer pressure. It gets more and more difficult for us to be able to stay on the straight and narrow. So what is burnout? Well, it's a state of emotional, physical and mental exhaustion. You know, and you can see there in the middle that wellbeing is that we're taking care of all of those parts of our world. You know, it often results in us feeling overwhelmed, undervalued or lacking control over our environment. You know, one of the symptoms, well, what is it that we see from people? Now we see fatigue, you know, irritable, reduced performance, you know, a sense of detachment.

And the question I asked myself is, have I experienced burnout? I'm not sure. Now, I want to try and explain certainly my personal story a little bit. You know, I played professional tennis. I had an amazing US college experience. Just absolutely loved the feeling I got, the purpose, the value that I felt I was able to have on people's lives. You know, it was something that just, I never quite got that as a player. And as a coach, there's that initial purpose, you're getting paid all of a sudden, you know, as a somewhat failed tennis player, I was used to having no money.
